source.title: Early Stopping in Deep Networks: Double Descent and How to Eliminate it

page_placements.theme: Different feature-learning speeds can generate epoch-wise peaks

record.tranche_reason: Tests epoch-wise double descent using theoretical analysis and experiments on regression models and CNNs; it also refines the proposed effective-complexity explanation.
record.gate_note: The paper tests epoch-wise risk/test error and reports results for step-size changes. It does not test model-size or sample-size sweeps. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study's own theory and experiments show epoch-wise double descent (V2) in least squares, a two-layer ReLU net, a 5-layer CNN and ResNet-18. It argues explicitly that the effective-complexity conjecture (V5) is the wrong explanation on the epoch axis and replaces it with a superposition of bias-variance tradeoffs. That is a specific argument that V5 needs restating, so T5 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that epoch-wise double descent comes from a superposition of bias-variance tradeoffs, because different features or layers are learned at different speeds. It is not caused by training time controlling effective model complexity. Rescaling step sizes (or initialization) eliminates or mitigates it and improves early-stopping performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines epoch-wise behavior, including the noisy-CIFAR setting used in prior work, and adds layer-specific step-size adjustments; it does not reproduce model-size or sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The occurrence and strength of epoch-wise double descent change with feature or layer step sizes and, in the two-layer network, initialization scales.

fits_no_version.finding: Rescaling per-layer or per-feature step sizes so the bias-variance tradeoffs align removes epoch-wise double descent and lowers the best early-stopped test error. Shown in least squares (Prop. 1), the two-layer net, the 5-layer CNN and ResNet-18.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Epoch-wise double descent arises from different model parts being learned at different speeds; equalizing their learning speeds removes it and improves early stopping.

record.problems: The CNN and ResNet test-error curves are reported in figures without numeric values or uncertainty estimates. The deep-network experiments use one stated label-noise level, 20%, and do not sweep data size or model size.
record.rows_left_out: No reported claim-relevant results were omitted.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep; model-wise double descent is only cited.
No sweep over the number of training samples.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
Peak location along the size and sample axes; no effective-complexity measure is computed and compared with peak location.
No label-noise sweep (one level, 20%) and no tuned ℓ2 regularization. The paper notes that more than two tradeoffs could superpose, but multiple peaks are not shown.

missing.what: Simulated risk of early-stopped least squares (d=700, n=5d and 10d), averaged over 100 runs with ±1 std. The only result with uncertainty; it validates the analytic risk curve that underlies R1/R2.
Explicit statement that epoch-wise double descent is not tied to overparameterization and occurs in both under- and overparameterized models.

record.verdict_notes: T5 is chosen because the paper's central claim restates V5 for the epoch axis. The study is not an original source. The record's 'uncertainty_reported: y' holds only for Appendix A's Figure 7; the CNN and ResNet curves have no error bars or numbers. The V2 support for the CNN and ResNet-18 reproduces the setting of Nakkiran et al. (one of the original sources), so it is close to a replication.

versions.untested_parts: The empirical deep-network results concern noisy CIFAR-10; the paper does not test every architecture, dataset, or training regime.
No sweep over the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold.
The study does not test a capacity sweep across model classes.
The paper challenges the effective-complexity explanation for epoch-wise double descent, but does not test whether one measure predicts peak locations along model-size or sample-size axes.
No systematic comparison of label-noise levels or optimally tuned regularization is reported; the CNN experiments use 20% random label noise.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameter number is reported.
